The braided monoidal structure of tube algebra representations
David Jaklitsch, Makoto Yamashita

Abstract
We consider the tube algebra of a spherical semisimple multitensor category 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , and construct a braided monoidal structure with twist for its representations. We further show that this category is braided tensor equivalent with the Drinfeld center of the ind-category of 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , extending the well-known linear equivalence.



\DefineSimpleKey

bibhow

1
Introduction

Tube algebras
first appeared in the work of Ocneanu
[
23
]
on the structure of subfactors and associated topological quantum field theory.
This construction was analogous to the quantum double of Hopf algebras, and a precise connection between the Drinfeld center of the associated tensor category was clarified through the work of Izumi
[
15
]
and Müger
[
20
]
.
To be precise, these works show that, given a unitary fusion category
\mathcal{X}
, the linear category of modules over Ocneanu’s tube algebra
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})
is equivalent to the underlying linear category of the Drinfeld center category
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{X})
.
This correspondence has been generalized to the setting without finiteness assumption on the number of irreducible classes, and expanded to annular algebras when
\mathcal{X}
is a rigid C
∗
-tensor category as studied in
[
12
,
21
]
, which gave a linear equivalence of between
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})
-modules and the Drinfeld center.

While it is possible to transport the braided monoidal structure of
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{X})
to
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})
-modules via this equivalence, in view of the connection to the Levin–Wen type lattice models
[
5
,
13
]
, it is desirable to have a direct description of fusion and braiding on the category of modules over the tube algebra, as conjectured in
[
9
]
.
In this direction, Das, Ghosh, and Gupta
[
6
]
showed that, starting from a shaded planar algebra (equivalent to a unitary rigid
2
-category
\mathcal{X}
generated by a single
1
-cell), the unitary representations of the associated annular algebra has a structure of unitary braided category, and that a certain subcategory of ‘finite modules’ is braided equivalent to the Drinfeld center
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{X})
.
A similar claim can be found in
[
14
]
, although precise details seems to be missing there.

In this paper we relax the unitarity, single generation, and finiteness assumptions, and establish a corresponding comparison result.
That is, we define a braided monoidal structure on the category of modules over the tube algebra
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
of a pivotal
2
-category
\mathcal{X}
and a generating set
\mathrm{I}
of objects (
1
-cells).
Our main result (Theorem
5.3
) shows that this indeed recovers the (ribbon) braided monoidal category
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{X})
.

Our model of monoidal product and braiding is loosely motivated by the topological presentation of corresponding structures on the fusion ring in
[
23
]
.
We hope that this gives a more intuitive description of topological operations on the Levin–Wen type lattice models than the conventional ones, as in
[
6
]
, based on string diagrams.

The outline of paper is as follows.
In Section
2
, we review some basic materials on rigid
2
-categories.
In Section
3
, we set up a graphical calculus scheme adapted from the standard topological presentation of
2
-categories and planar algebra theory.
In Section
4
, we define the monoidal structure and braiding on the category of modules over the tube algebra, using our scheme from Section
3
.
Finally in Section
5
, we carry out the comparison with the Drinfeld center.

2
Preliminaries

2.1
Spherical multitensor categories

Let us begin with a quick review of the basic concepts on multitensor categories, mostly following the convention of
[
8
]
.

Let
\Bbbk
be an algebraically closed field.
A
multitensor category over
\Bbbk
is a locally finite
\Bbbk
-linear abelian category
\mathcal{X}
together with a rigid monoidal structure, such that the tensor product
\otimes
is bilinear on morphisms.
Without loss of generality we may and do assume
\mathcal{X}
to be strict, in view of MacLane’s coherence theorem.

We have the canonical irreducible decomposition of monoidal the unit,

\mathbf{1}=\bigoplus_{i\in\Gamma}\mathbf{1}_{i}

for the finite set
\Gamma
parametrizing the primitive idempotents of the semisimple commutative algebra
\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1})
.
This induces the corresponding decomposition of the category

\mathcal{X}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in\Gamma}\mathcal{X}_{ij},

where the subcategory
\mathcal{X}_{ij}\subset\mathcal{X}
consists of the objects
x
satisfying
x\cong\mathbf{1}_{i}\otimes x\otimes\mathbf{1}_{j}
.
We use the notation
\mathcal{X}_{i}\coloneqq\mathcal{X}_{ii}
for the diagonal tensor categories. We freely identify
\mathcal{X}
with the associated
2
-category, whose
0
-cells are elements of
\Gamma
,
1
-cells are objects of
\mathcal{X}_{ij}
, and
2
-cells are morphisms of
\mathcal{X}_{ij}
. The horizontal composition is given by the tensor product
[
8
, Remark 4.3.7]
.

A
pivotal structure
on
\mathcal{X}
is given by a monoidal natural isomorphism from the identity functor of
\mathcal{X}
to the double dual functor, i.e., a natural family of isomorphisms

p_{x}\colon x\xrightarrow{\sim}x^{**}

compatible with the natural isomorphism
(x\otimes y)^{**}\cong x^{**}\otimes y^{**}
.
By
[
22
, Theorem 2.2]
, we may assume that
p
is strict, meaning that
(x\otimes y)^{*}=y^{*}\otimes x^{*}
and
p_{x}=\mathrm{id}_{x}
.
We also identify left and right duals, i.e., for every
x\in\mathcal{X}
we may assume

x^{*}={}^{*}x,

and write
\overline{x}
for this object.
We can thus denote the corresponding evaluation and coevaluation morphisms by

\displaystyle{\mathrm{ev}}_{x}

\displaystyle\colon\overline{x}\otimes x\to\mathbf{1},

\displaystyle{\mathrm{coev}}_{x}

\displaystyle\colon\mathbf{1}\to x\otimes\overline{x},

\displaystyle\overline{{\,\mathrm{ev}}}_{x}

\displaystyle\colon x\otimes\overline{x}\to\mathbf{1},

\displaystyle\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{x}

\displaystyle\colon\mathbf{1}\to\overline{x}\otimes x.

These allow us to define left and right traces of an endomorphism
f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(x,x)
as

\mathrm{tr}_{x}^{\mathrm{r}}(f)\coloneqq\overline{{\,\mathrm{ev}}}_{x}\circ(f\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\mathrm{coev}_{x},\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathrm{tr}_{x}^{\mathrm{l}}(f)\coloneqq\mathrm{ev}_{x}\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes f)\circ\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{x}\,.

In a pivotal multitensor category,
\overline{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ji}
holds for a homogeneous object
x\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
. In that case, we have that
\mathrm{tr}_{x}^{\mathrm{r}}(f)\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}\!\left(\mathbf{1}_{j},\mathbf{1}_{j}\right)
and
\mathrm{tr}_{x}^{\mathrm{l}}(f)\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}\!\left(\mathbf{1}_{i},\mathbf{1}_{i}\right)
. We identify these traces as scalars in the base field via the unique unital isomorphism of
\Bbbk
-algebras

\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}\!\left(\mathbf{1}_{i},\mathbf{1}_{i}\right)\xrightarrow{~\sim~}\Bbbk\,,\quad\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}_{i}}\mapsto 1\,.

(2.1)

Another consequence of the pivotal structure is the equality

((\overline{{\,\mathrm{ev}}}_{x}\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathrm{ev}_{y}\otimes\mathrm{id}))\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes f\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes((\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathrm{coev}_{x}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{y}))=f

(2.2)

for
f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(x,y)
.

Definition 2.1

(cf.
[
19
,
4
]
)
.

A pivotal multitensor category
\mathcal{X}
is called
spherical
when left and right traces coincide under (
2.1
) for every endomorphism of
f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}_{ij}}(x,x)
, for all
i,j\in\Gamma
and all
x\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
. In that case, we denote this scalar by
\mathrm{tr}_{x}(f)
.

The
dimension
of an object
x\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
is the scalar

\mathrm{d}_{x}\coloneq\mathrm{tr}_{x}(\mathrm{id}_{x})
. Sphericality ensures that the dimension of dual objects obey
\mathrm{d}_{\overline{x}}=\mathrm{d}_{x}
.

The sphericality condition in Definition
2.1
is equivalent to the following
[
19
, Proposition 5.8]
:
for any fixed
i_{0}\in\Gamma
, the rigid tensor category
\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}}
is spherical, and for each
j\in\Gamma
and any fixed irreducible object
x\in\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}j}
, the Frobenius algebra
Q=x\otimes\overline{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}}
is normalized in the sense of
[
19
, Definition 3.13]
.

Remark 2.2
.

In the finite setting, given a spherical fusion category
\mathcal{X}
there is a pivotal
2
-category
\mathbf{Mod}^{\mathrm{sph}}(\mathcal{X})
of spherical module categories over
\mathcal{X}
as defined in
[
10
, Section 3.6]
and
[
11
, Definition 5.22]
. By considering a choice of simple objects in this semisimple
2
-category as indexing set
\Gamma
, we obtain a spherical multifusion category as in Definition
2.1
.
Reciprocally, given a spherical multifusion category
\mathcal{X}
, we have that
\mathcal{X}_{i}
is a spherical fusion category for any
i\in\Gamma
. Moreover, the (idempotent completed
[
7
]
)
2
-category associated to
\mathcal{X}
can be realized as as a subcategory of the
2
-category
\mathbf{Mod}^{\mathrm{sph}}(\mathcal{X}_{i})
.

Throughout the paper we will tacitly assume that
\mathcal{X}
is semisimple and spherical.
In particular, any object of
\mathcal{X}
is a direct sum of simple objects, but we allow for
\mathcal{X}
to have infinitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects.

We fix for each
i,j\in\Gamma
a set
\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
(resp.
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
) of representatives of isomorphism classes of objects (resp. simple objects) in
\mathcal{X}_{ij}
.

We will use the following notation

x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n}\equiv x_{1}\cdots x_{n}

in order to shorten lengthy expressions involving the tensor product of several objects in
\mathcal{X}
.
In order to simplify the presentation, we assume these objects to be from homogeneous components
\mathcal{X}_{ij}
.
In this case, the above product is nontrivial if and only if each object
x_{k}
belongs to
\mathcal{X}_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}
, and is nonzero, for some choice of
0
-cells
i_{1},\ldots,i_{n+1}\in\Gamma
.

2.2
Ind-completion

The
ind-completion
of a category
\mathcal{X}
is the category
\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
whose objects are colimits of filtered diagrams in
\mathcal{X}
.
Concretely, one can represent its objects by functors
F\colon I\to\mathcal{X}
where
I
is a filtered category, and with morphism spaces between two such functors given by

\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}}(F,G)\coloneqq{\lim}_{i}\mathrm{colim}_{j}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(F(i),G(j)).

When
\mathcal{X}
is a semisimple
\Bbbk
-linear category, every object in
\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
is a formal direct product of objects in
\mathcal{X}
, that is,

\bigoplus_{a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}V_{a}\otimes a

(2.3)

for a collection of vector spaces
V_{a}
labeled by the irreducible classes, and the morphism space between two such objects is given by

\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}}\biggl(\bigoplus_{a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}V_{a}\otimes a,\bigoplus_{a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}W_{a}\otimes a\biggr)=\prod_{a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\operatorname{Hom}(V_{a},W_{a}).

Indeed, (
2.3
) can be considered as the colimit of diagram
F\colon I\to\mathcal{X}
where
I
is the category whose objects are
V^{\prime}=\bigoplus_{a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}V^{\prime}_{a}
, a direct sum of subspaces
V^{\prime}_{a}\subset V_{a}
for
a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
such that
\dim V^{\prime}<\infty
, ordered by inclusion.
Conversely, suppose we are given a filtered diagram
F\colon I\to\mathcal{X}
.
Then, for each fixed
a\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, the finite-dimensional vector spaces
\operatorname{Hom}(a,F(i))
form a directed system.
Writing
V_{a}
for its colimit, we see that (
2.3
) is a presentation of the overall colimit of
F
.

Furthermore, when
\mathcal{X}
is a multitensor category, the
\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
inherits from
\mathcal{X}
a monoidal structure with the same set of
0
-cells.
However,
\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
is not rigid since we are allowing infinite direct sums of
\mathbf{1}
, among others, as its objects.

2.3
Drinfeld center

Next, let us recall the
Drinfeld center

\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X})
of the multitensor category
\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
for a semisimple multitensor category, cf.
[
18
,
21
]
.
Its objects are pairs
(Z,\sigma^{Z})
, where
Z\in\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
and
\sigma^{Z}
is a natural isomorphism

\sigma^{Z}_{X}\colon X\otimes Z\to Z\otimes X

obeying the corresponding hexagon axiom.
The centrality condition against
X=\mathbf{1}
shows that
Z
must be of the form
\bigoplus_{i\in\Gamma}Z_{i}
for
Z_{i}\in\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}_{i}
.
Moreover,
\sigma^{Z}
is completely determined by its action on objects of
\mathcal{X}_{ij}
for
i,j\in\Gamma
, so that our data can be represented by natural isomorphisms

\sigma^{Z}_{a}\colon a\otimes Z_{j}\to Z_{i}\otimes a\quad(i,j\in\Gamma,a\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}).

Morphisms in
\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X})
are morphisms in
\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}
between the underlying objects that commute with the respective half-braidings.

Of course, we can restrict to the case
Z_{i}\in\mathcal{X}_{i}
, which gives the category
\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{X})
.
If we further assume that
\mathcal{X}
is a tensor category, we recover the usual definition of the Drinfeld center category.

The monoidal product of
\mathcal{X}
induces a monoidal structure on
\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X})
where the underlying object of
Z\otimes Z^{\prime}
is given by
(Z_{i}\otimes Z^{\prime}_{i})_{i\in\Gamma}
, endowed with the composition of the respective half-braidings.
Moreover,
\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X})
is a braided category, whose braiding
(X,\sigma^{X})\otimes(Y,\sigma^{Y})\to(Y,\sigma^{Y})\otimes(X,\sigma^{X})
is given by

\sigma_{X,Y}=\sigma^{Y}_{X}\colon X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X,

i.e., the action of the half-braiding on
Y
.

Under the rigidity assumption on
\mathcal{X}
, for each
i\in\Gamma
, the restriction functor
\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X})\to\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X}_{i})
given by
Z\mapsto Z_{i}
are braided monoidal equivalences, see
[
24
,
19
]
.

2.4
Algebras with local units

To work with tube algebras in the infinite setting, we will need to forgo assuming the existence of a unit.

Definition 2.3

(
[
1
,
2
]
)
.

An associative
\Bbbk
-algebra with local units
consists of a
\Bbbk
-vector space
A
together with a product, i.e., a linear map
\cdot\colon A\otimes A\to A
obeying the following properties.

•

Associativity: for every
f,g,h\in A

f\cdot(g\cdot h)=(f\cdot g)\cdot h

•

Local units: for every finite dimensional vector subspace
V\subset A
there exists an idempotent
e\in A
such that
V\subset eAe
.

Similar to the case of unital algebras, there is an associated notion of representation for algebras with local units.

Definition 2.4
.

Let
A
be an associative
\Bbbk
-algebra with local units.

(i)

A
locally presented

(
right
)
representation
of
A
is a
\Bbbk
-vector space
M
together with a module action, i.e., a linear map
M\otimes A\to M,m\otimes f\mapsto m.f
fulfilling the following properties.

•

Module associativity:
m.(f\cdot g)=(m.f).g
for
m\in M
and
f,g\in A
.

•

Locality: for every finite dimensional vector subspace
W\subset M
there exists an idempotent
e\in A
such that
W.e=W
.

(ii)

A
morphism of locally presented representations
is simply a module homomorphism, i.e., a linear map
F\colon M\to N
obeying
F(m.f)=F(m).f
for
m\in M
and
f\in A
.

(iii)

We denote by
\operatorname{Rep}A
the
\Bbbk
-linear category of locally presented representations over
A
.

3
Graphical calculus and spaces of tubes

3.1
Cyclically invariant vector spaces of morphisms

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a pivotal multitensor category. In the spirit of
[
3
]
, we define in this section a cyclically invariant vector space of morphisms.
Let
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
be objects of
\mathcal{X}
.
Then the vector space
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x_{1}\cdots x_{n})
only depends on the cyclic order of
(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})
up to canonical isomorphism.
We will mostly consider the case where
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
are homogeneous and
cyclically composable
, in the sense that
x_{k}\in\mathcal{X}_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}
with
i_{n+1}=i_{1}
.

To make this more precise, consider an indexing category
\mathfrak{n}
whose objects are
\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
and with a unique isomorphism between every pair of objects. We define a
\mathfrak{n}
-shaped diagram of finite dimensional vector spaces

\mathrm{X}\colon\mathfrak{n}\to\mathrm{Vec}_{\Bbbk},\qquad i\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x_{i}\cdots x_{n}x_{1}\cdots x_{i-1})

assigning to the unique isomorphism between
i
and
i+1
the isomorphism

\displaystyle\mathrm{X}_{i,i+1}\colon\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x_{i}\cdots x_{n}x_{1}\cdots x_{i-1})

\displaystyle\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x_{i+1}\cdots x_{n}x_{1}\cdots x_{i-1}x_{i})

(3.1)

\displaystyle f

\displaystyle\mapsto(\mathrm{ev}_{x_{i}}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes f\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{x_{i}}

Equalities of the form (
2.2
) ensure that the composition
\mathrm{X}_{n,1}\circ\cdots\circ\mathrm{X}_{1,2}
equals the identity map of the vector space
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x_{1}\cdots x_{n})
. The identification of the double-dual of a tensor product as the product of the double-duals implies the functoriality of
\mathrm{X}
.

Definition 3.1
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a pivotal multitensor category and
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
cyclically composable objects in
\mathcal{X}
.
Define the
vector space of morphisms bounded by
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
as the limit

\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\right]\mathclose{}\coloneqq\lim\mathrm{X}

(3.2)

in the category
\mathrm{Vec}_{\Bbbk}
of finite-dimensional vector spaces.

Remark 3.2
.

By construction the vector space (
3.2
) is invariant under cyclic permutations of
(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})
, thus we canonically identify

\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\right]\mathclose{}=\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{2}\cdots x_{n}x_{1}\right]\mathclose{}=\cdots=\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{n}x_{1}\cdots x_{n-1}\right]\mathclose{}.

As remarked before, we will be mostly interested in the case when each
x_{k}
is homogeneous, that is,
x_{k}\in\mathcal{X}_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}
for
i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in\Gamma
, with the convention
i_{n+1}=i_{1}
.
We thus identify
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}_{i_{1}}}(\mathbf{1}_{i_{1}},x_{1}\cdots x_{n})
with
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}_{i_{2}}}(\mathbf{1}_{i_{2}},x_{2}\cdots x_{n}x_{1})
, etc., by the maps of the form (
3.1
), and call this
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\right]\mathclose{}
.

Rigidity allows us to define a composition relative to an object
b\in\mathcal{X}
via the following map

\displaystyle\circ_{b}\colon\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}\left(\mathbf{1},x\overline{b}\,\right)\otimes\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},by)

\displaystyle\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},xy),

(3.3)

\displaystyle(f,g)

\displaystyle\mapsto(\mathrm{id}_{x}\otimes\mathrm{ev}_{b}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{y})\circ(f\otimes g).

The composition map (
3.3
) relative to an object
b\in\mathcal{X}
, via the isomorphisms (
3.1
), descends to a map between cyclically invariant vector spaces

\circ_{b}\colon\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\,\overline{b}\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[b\,y\right]\mathclose{}\to\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\,y\right]\mathclose{}

(3.4)

In the case that
\mathcal{X}
is semisimple, these induce an isomorphism

\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\circ_{t}\colon\bigoplus_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\,\overline{t}\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[t\,y\right]\mathclose{}\xrightarrow{\;\cong\;}\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\,y\right]\mathclose{}

Remark 3.3
.

For each object
x\in\mathcal{X}
consider the universal limit cone defining
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}x\right]\mathclose{}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}x\right]\mathclose{}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},\overline{x}x)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x\overline{x})}
(
3.1
)

the image of
\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{x}
under the vertical isomorphism is the coevaluation morphism
\mathrm{coev}_{x}
.
We denote their common inverse image in
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}x\right]\mathclose{}=\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
by
\mathtt{e}_{x}
, and refer to it as
the unit morphism of
x
. This morphism serves as identity of relative composition (
3.4
) as shown in Lemma
3.4
.

The unit morphism of
x\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
can also be used to define

partial traces
: given
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[yx\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}

\mathrm{ptr}_{x}(f)\coloneqq f\circ_{x\overline{x}}\,\mathtt{e}_{x}\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[y\right]\mathclose{}

Full traces
, or simply
traces
are similarly defined for
endomorphisms

f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
with
x\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
by

\mathrm{tr}_{x}(f)\coloneqq f\circ_{x\overline{x}}\,\mathtt{e}_{x}\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\mathbf{1}_{i}\right]\mathclose{}\overset{\eqref{scalar_id}}{\cong}\Bbbk\,.

(A word of caution: for arbitrary
x\in\mathcal{X}
we have natural isomorphisms
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}\cong\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
, but
\mathrm{tr}_{x}(f)
and
\mathrm{tr}_{\overline{x}}(f)
are different elements of
\Bbbk^{\Gamma}
.
When
x\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
, these elements have only one nonzero components, respectively at
i
-th and
j
-th components, which are the same scalars.)

Lemma 3.4
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a pivotal multitensor category.

(
i
)

The unit morphism of an object
x\in\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
obeys

\mathtt{e}_{x}=\mathtt{e}_{\overline{x}},\quad\mathtt{e}_{xy}=\mathtt{e}_{x}\circ_{\mathbf{1}_{j}}\mathtt{e}_{y},\qquad\text{ and }\qquad f\circ_{x}\mathtt{e}_{x}=f\,\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[yx\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}\,,

for any
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[yx\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
, which justifies its name.

(
ii
)

Given
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{y}\right]\mathclose{}
and
g\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[yz\right]\mathclose{}
, it holds that

f\circ_{y}g=g\circ_{\overline{y}}f

as elements of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xz\right]\mathclose{}
.

(
iii
)

For
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[w\overline{x}\,\overline{y}\right]\mathclose{}
and
g\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[yxz\right]\mathclose{}
, it holds that

f\circ_{xy}g=\mathrm{ptr}_{x}(f\circ_{y}g)=\mathrm{ptr}_{y}(f\circ_{x}g)

as elements of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xz\right]\mathclose{}
.

(
iv
)

For
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xy_{1}y_{2}\right]\mathclose{}
,
g\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{y}_{1}w\right]\mathclose{}
and
h\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{y}_{2}z\right]\mathclose{}
, it holds that

(g\circ_{y_{1}}f)\circ_{\overline{y}_{2}}h=g\circ_{y_{1}}(f\circ_{\overline{y}_{2}}h)

as elements of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xwz\right]\mathclose{}
.

Proof.

Statement (i) follows from
\mathrm{coev}_{\overline{x}}=\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{x}
.
Next, for (ii), take
f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x\overline{y})
and
g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},y\overline{z})
.
We then have the equality

f\circ_{y}g=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathrm{ev}_{y}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(f\otimes g)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\overline{{\,\mathrm{ev}}}_{y}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ(g\otimes f)

in
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xz\right]\mathclose{}
.
Item (iii) follows from the standard snake relations for the structure morphisms of duality.
Finally, (iv) follows from associativity of the composition in
\mathcal{X}
and uses the fact that the double dual of a tensor product is the product of the double duals.
∎

3.2
Diagrammatic calculus

We set up the conventions for a graphical calculus using the
2
-dimensional graphical representation of
2
-categories (which in a sense is the dual graph to the usual string diagram for tensor categories).

First, a
0
-cell
i\in\Gamma
is depicted by a vertex.
Properly speaking, vertices should be decorated by the labels
i\in\Gamma
, but we supress this from our diagrams.

Next, a
1
-cell, that is, a homogeneous object
x\in\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
will be depicted by an oriented line segment.
Changing the orientation of the edge results in changing the label by the dual object.

3.3
Spherical pairing

Throughout this section we assume that
\mathcal{X}
is a spherical semisimple multitensor category.
The pivotal structure of
\mathcal{X}
induces an important structure on the Hom-spaces of
\mathcal{X}
, namely a non-degenerate pairing: for any
x,y\in\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}_{ij}

\displaystyle\langle-,-\rangle_{x,y}\colon\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\overline{x},\overline{y})

\displaystyle\otimes\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(x,y)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1}_{j},\mathbf{1}_{j})\cong\Bbbk,

(3.5)

\displaystyle(f,g)

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathrm{ev}_{y}\circ(f\otimes g)\circ\overline{{\mathrm{coev}}}_{x}=\overline{{\,\mathrm{ev}}}_{y}\circ(g\otimes f)\circ\mathrm{coev}_{x}\,.

We extend this to arbitrary
x,y\in\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
by bilinearity, noting that
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(x,y)
is the direct sum of spaces
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}_{ij}}(x_{ij},y_{ij})
with
x=\bigoplus_{i,j}x_{ij}
for
x_{ij}\in\mathcal{X}_{ij}
, and a similar decomposition for
y
.
In particular, we have for the vector space
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1},x)
that the pairing

\langle-,-\rangle_{\mathbf{1},x}=\circ_{x}
is the composition relative to
x
.

A direct computation involving the sphericality of the pivotal structure of
\mathcal{X}
proves that the pairing (
3.5
) commutes with the isomorphisms
\mathrm{X}_{i,i+1}
from equation (
3.1
).
Consequently, when
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}
is a cyclically composable sequence of
1
-cells, (
3.5
) descends to a pairing on
\mathrm{H}
spaces

\langle-,-\rangle=\mathrm{tr}_{x_{n}}(-\circ_{x_{1}\cdots x_{n-1}}-)\colon\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}_{n}\cdots\overline{x}_{1}\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\right]\mathclose{}\to\Bbbk

(3.6)

where we interpret the value of
\mathrm{tr}_{x_{n}}
as a scalar by the isomorphism
\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{1}_{i})\to\Bbbk
as in (
2.1
).
The non-degeneracy of the pairing means that
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\right]\mathclose{}^{*}\cong\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}_{n}\cdots\overline{x}_{1}\right]\mathclose{}
.

Definition 3.5
.

Let
\alpha=\{\alpha^{i}\}
and
\overline{\alpha}=\{\overline{\alpha}_{i}\}
be bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ax\right]\mathclose{}
and
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}\,\overline{a}\right]\mathclose{}
respectively. The bases
(\alpha,\overline{\alpha})
are called
a
pair of dual bases
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ax\right]\mathclose{}
with respect to (
3.6
) when
\langle\overline{\alpha}_{i},\alpha^{j}\rangle=\delta_{ij}
holds.

Given a pair of dual bases
(\alpha,\overline{\alpha})
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ax\right]\mathclose{}
, the linear map defined by

\displaystyle\Bbbk

\displaystyle\to\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}\,\overline{a}\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[a\,x\right]\mathclose{}

(3.7)

\displaystyle 1

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{i}\;\overline{\alpha}_{i}\otimes\alpha^{i}

is independent of the choice of dual bases. The element
\sum_{i}\overline{\alpha}_{i}\otimes\alpha^{i}
will be depicted by

\blacktriangleright
\blacktriangleright
\blacktriangleright
\blacktriangleright
x
a
a
x
\overline{\alpha}_{i}
\otimes
\alpha^{i}

where the sum over the basis elements is implicit and indicated by Einstein’s summation convention.

(3.8)

where
(\alpha,\overline{\alpha})
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ax\right]\mathclose{}
and
(\beta,\overline{\beta})
dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}x\right]\mathclose{}
.

Composition relative to an object is compatible with the pairing only up to a dimension factor. For a simple object
x\in\operatorname{Irr}\,\mathcal{X}_{ij}
, define

f\bullet_{x}g\coloneqq\sqrt{\mathrm{d}_{x}}\;f\circ_{x}g\,.

For composable simple objects
x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}

f\bullet_{x_{1}\cdots x_{n}}g\coloneqq\sqrt{\mathrm{d}_{x_{1}}\cdots\mathrm{d}_{x_{n}}}\;f\circ_{x_{1}\cdots x_{n}}g\,.

Lemma 3.7

(
[
3
, Lemma 1.1]
)
.

Let
y\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
be a simple object, and
a,b\in\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
homogeneous objects.

(i)

For
f\in{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ay\right]\mathclose{}}
and
g\in{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{y}\,\overline{a}\right]\mathclose{}}
, then

\mathrm{d}_{y}\,f\circ_{a}g=\langle f,g\rangle\mathtt{e}_{y}\;.

(ii)

Dominance relation: unit morphisms can be decomposed in terms of sums of dual bases over simple objects.

(3.9)

(iii)

For
f\in{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ay\right]\mathclose{}},\;g\in{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{y}\,b\right]\mathclose{}},\;h\in{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\,y\right]\mathclose{}},~\text{and}~k\in{\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{y}\,\overline{a}\right]\mathclose{}}

\langle f\bullet_{y}g,h\bullet_{y}k\rangle=\langle f,k\rangle\cdot\langle g,h\rangle\;.

Proof.

Since
y
is simple,
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[y\overline{y}\right]\mathclose{}
is one dimensional and thus
f\circ_{a}g=\lambda\,\mathtt{e}_{y}
for a scalar
\lambda\in\Bbbk
. It follows that
\langle f,g\rangle=\mathrm{tr}_{y}(f\circ_{a}g)=\lambda\,\mathrm{d}_{y}
which implies (i). To prove (ii) first assume that
b=\mathbf{1}
and
a=y
is simple. Notice that, from Schur’s lemma,
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[t\overline{y}\right]\mathclose{}
is one-dimensional only if
t\cong y
and zero otherwise. It follows that the sum on the left hand side of (
3.9
) reduces to

\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\mathrm{d}_{t}\,\overline{\alpha}_{t,i}\circ_{t}\alpha_{t}^{i}=\mathrm{d}_{y}\,\overline{\alpha}_{y}\circ_{t}\alpha_{y}=\langle\overline{\alpha}_{y},\alpha_{y}\rangle\,\mathtt{e}_{y}=\mathtt{e}_{y}

where the second to last equality follows from (i) and the last one holds since
\overline{\alpha}_{y}
and
\alpha_{y}
are dual bases. Due to semisimplicty of
\mathcal{X}
, extending the argument to direct sums ensures that the whole statement holds. Lastly, notice that

\langle f\bullet_{y}g,h\bullet_{y}k\rangle=\mathrm{d}_{y}\,\mathrm{tr}_{a}(f\circ_{y}g\circ_{b}h\circ_{y}k)\overset{\rm(i)}{=}\mathrm{d}_{y}\,\frac{\langle g,h\rangle}{\mathrm{d}_{y}}\mathrm{tr}_{a}(f\circ_{y}\mathtt{e}_{y}\circ_{y}k)=\langle f,k\rangle\cdot\langle g,h\rangle

which proves (iii).
∎

Lemma 3.8
.

Let
a,b,c
be homogeneous objects in
\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
.

(
i
)

For each
t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
consider a pair of dual bases
(\psi_{t},\overline{\psi}_{t})
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[atc\right]\mathclose{}
, and
(\beta_{t},\overline{\beta}_{t})
a pair of bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[b\overline{t}\right]\mathclose{}
. Then

\{\beta_{t}^{i}\bullet_{t}\psi_{t}^{j}\}_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}
and
\{\overline{\beta}_{t,i}\bullet_{t}\overline{\psi}_{t,j}\}_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}

is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[abc\right]\mathclose{}
.

(
ii
)

Given a pair of dual bases
(\varphi_{t},\overline{\varphi}_{t})
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[btc\right]\mathclose{}
, of each
t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, and
(\alpha_{t},\overline{\alpha}_{t})
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[a\overline{t}\right]\mathclose{}
. Then
\{\alpha_{t}^{i}\bullet_{t}\varphi_{t}^{j}\}_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}
and
\{\overline{\alpha}_{t,i}\bullet_{t}\overline{\varphi}_{t,j}\}_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[abc\right]\mathclose{}
.

Thus, graphically we have in the vector space
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[abc\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{abc}\right]\mathclose{}
that

for an arbitrary pair of dual bases
(\gamma,\overline{\gamma})
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[abc\right]\mathclose{}
.

Proof.

From Lemma
3.7
(iii) follows that

\langle\,\overline{\beta}_{t,i}\bullet_{t}\overline{\psi}_{t,j},\beta_{s}^{k}\bullet_{s}\psi_{s}^{l}\,\rangle=\langle\overline{\beta}_{t,i},\beta_{s}^{k}\rangle\cdot\langle\overline{\psi}_{t,j},\psi_{s}^{l}\rangle=\delta_{t,s}\delta_{i,k}\delta_{j,l}

where the
\delta_{t,s}
appears after taking into account that
\overline{\beta}_{t,i}\circ_{b}\beta_{s}^{k}
belongs to
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[t\overline{s}\right]\mathclose{}\cong\delta_{t,s}\Bbbk
. The additional delta factors come since we are pairing pairs of dual bases. This proves (i). Statement (ii) follows analogously.
∎

In the case that a graph has two edges with labels dual to each other, we can resolve them over simple objects, via the composition:

\star_{x}\colon\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[axb\overline{x}c\right]\mathclose{}\xrightarrow{\eqref{eq:dual_bases}}\bigoplus_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[axb\overline{x}c\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{t}\right]\mathclose{}\otimes\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{x}t\right]\mathclose{}\xrightarrow{\bullet_{x}\;\otimes\;\bullet_{\,\overline{x}}}\bigoplus_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[atb\overline{t}c\right]\mathclose{}

This operation can be graphically represented as follows. For
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[axb\overline{x}c\right]\mathclose{}
, the homogeneous component of
\star_{x}(f)
associated to
t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
is given by

where
(\alpha_{t},\overline{\alpha}_{t})
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\overline{t}\right]\mathclose{}
.

Lemma 3.9
.

The maps
\star_{x}
satisfy the following consistency conditions.

(
i
)

Given
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{y}xyz\right]\mathclose{}
and
g\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{z}\,w\right]\mathclose{}
, it holds in
\bigoplus_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xtw\overline{t}\right]\mathclose{}
that

\star_{y}(f\circ_{z}g)=\star_{y}(f)\circ_{z}g,\quad\text{ and }\quad\star_{y}(f\bullet_{z}g)=\star_{y}(f)\bullet_{z}g\,.

(3.10)

(
ii
)

Given
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[axyzb\overline{z}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
, it holds that

\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\star_{xt}(\star_{yz}(f)_{t})\,=\,\star_{xyz}(f)\,=\,\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\star_{tz}(\star_{xy}(f)_{t})

(3.11)

(
iii
)

Given
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[xyzw\overline{z}\,\overline{y}\right]\mathclose{}
, it holds that

\star_{z}(\star_{y}(f))=\star_{y}(\star_{z}(f))\,,

\star_{yz}(f)=\sum_{s,t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\star_{st}(\star_{z}(\star_{y}(f)_{s})_{t})=\sum_{s,t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\star_{st}(\star_{y}(\star_{z}(f)_{t})_{s})\,.

(
iv
)

For
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[ax\,\overline{b}\,\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
and
x\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, we have that
\star_{x}(f)=f
.

(
v
)

Given
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{z}\,\overline{y}\,\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}
, with
z\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, and families of pairs of dual bases
\alpha
,
\beta
,
\gamma
and
\eta
it holds

\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{d}_{t}\,\star_{xy}\left[\!\!\hbox to57.03pt{\vbox to64.82pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 28.51488pt\lower-13.81044pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

Proof.

The first statement follows from Lemma
3.4
, indeed

\star_{y}(f\circ_{z}g)=\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\alpha_{t}\circ_{b}(f\circ_{z}g)\circ_{\overline{b}}\overline{\alpha}_{t}=\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\alpha_{t}\circ_{b}(f\circ_{\overline{b}}\overline{\alpha}_{t})\circ_{z}g=\star_{y}(f)\circ_{z}g\,.

The second equality in (i) follows by considering the additional factor of
\sqrt{\mathrm{d}_{Z}}
.
To prove the second assertion, first notice that by (i) resolving a label over simple objects and gluing along a different label are procedures that commute. Now, by Lemma
3.8
, the two possible configurations of gluing pairs of dual bases agree. More explicitly, we have graphically for each simple object
s\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
that

3.4
Spaces of tubes and the Tube algebra

The rotational invariance of the graphical calculus allows for representing certain graphs as annuli or tubes:
two non-consecutive edges of a graph with the same label up to orientation reversal are merged. This leads to a loop labeled by the product of the labels of the edges in between the merged edges.

Definition 3.10
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a spherical semisimple multitensor category, and let
\mathrm{I}=\coprod_{i\in\Gamma}\mathrm{I}_{i}
and
\mathrm{J}=\coprod_{i,j\in\Gamma}\mathrm{J}_{ij}
be collections of isomorphism classes
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}_{i}\subset\mathrm{I}_{i}\subset\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}_{i}
and
\mathrm{J}_{ij}\subset\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
.

(i)

Given a pair of objects
a,b\in\mathrm{I}
, define the
space of tubes from
b
to
a
as the vector space

\mathrm{T}_{a;b}^{\mathrm{J}}\coloneqq\bigoplus_{x\in\mathrm{J}}\,\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\,\overline{x}\,a\,x\right]\mathclose{}

We refer to a vector
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\,\overline{x}\,a\,x\right]\mathclose{}
as a
tube element
and simply write
\mathrm{T}_{a;b}
for the choice
\mathrm{J}_{ij}=\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
.

(ii)

Given
a,b,c\in\mathrm{I}
, the
welding
of tube elements is defined by the map

\mathrm{w}\colon\mathrm{T}_{a;b}^{\mathrm{J}}\otimes\mathrm{T}_{b;c}^{\mathrm{J}}\to\mathrm{T}_{a;c}^{\mathrm{J}}

(3.12)

given for
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\overline{x}ax\right]\mathclose{}
and
g\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{c}\,\overline{y}by\right]\mathclose{}
by

We note that
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\overline{x}ax\right]\mathclose{}
is nontrivial only if
x\in\mathrm{J}_{ij}
holds for
i,j\in\Gamma

a\in\mathrm{I}_{ii}
,
b\in\mathrm{I}_{jj}
, so we ought to take the direct sum over this small choice of indexes, but supress it to avoid cumbersome notation.
In the following we will write
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}\subset\mathrm{I}
to mean
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}_{i}\subset\mathrm{I}_{i}
for
i\in\Gamma
, and similarly for
\mathrm{J}
.

Proposition 3.11
.

Welding of tube elements is associative, i.e., the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{T}_{a;b}^{\mathrm{J}}\otimes\mathrm{T}_{b;c}^{\mathrm{J}}\otimes\mathrm{T}_{c;d}^{\mathrm{J}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{T}_{a;b}^{\mathrm{J}}\otimes\mathrm{T}_{b;d}^{\mathrm{J}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{T}_{a;c}^{\mathrm{J}}\otimes\mathrm{T}_{c;d}^{\mathrm{J}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{T}_{a;d}^{\mathrm{J}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathrm{w}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{w}\otimes\mathrm{id}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{w}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{w}}

commutes for all
a,b,c,d\in\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
.

Proof.

Associativity follows from Lemma
3.9
. Indeed, given
f\in(\mathrm{T}_{a;b}^{\mathrm{J}})_{x}
,
g\in(\mathrm{T}_{b;c}^{\mathrm{J}})_{y}
and
h\in(\mathrm{T}_{c;d}^{\mathrm{J}})_{z}
we have on one hand that

\mathrm{w}(f\otimes\mathrm{w}(g\otimes h))=\mathrm{w}(f\otimes\star_{yz}(g\circ_{c}h))=\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\star_{xt}(f\circ_{b}\star_{yz}(g\circ_{c}h)_{t})\overset{\eqref{distr_star}}{=}\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\star_{xt}(\star_{yz}(f\circ_{b}g\circ_{c}h)_{t})

(3.13)

On the other hand, it holds that

\mathrm{w}(\mathrm{w}(f\otimes g)\otimes h)=\mathrm{w}(\star_{xy}(f\circ_{b}g)\otimes h)=\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\star_{tz}(\star_{xy}(f\circ_{b}g)_{t}\circ_{c}h)\overset{\eqref{distr_star}}{=}\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\star_{tz}(\star_{xy}(f\circ_{b}g\circ_{c}h)_{t})

(3.14)

The last steps in (
3.13
) and (
3.14
) are graphically depicted as

Remark 3.12
.

We will fix the label set to be
\mathrm{J}_{ij}=\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}_{ij}
.
This is intrinsically related to the following construction, see also Section
5
.
Given
a\in\mathcal{X}_{i}
and
j\in\Gamma
, we set

\mathrm{Z}_{j}(a)=\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}_{ij}}\,\overline{x}\otimes a\otimes x

in the ind-category of
\mathcal{X}_{jj}
.
Since
\mathcal{X}
is semisimple, this can be interpreted as a coend construction.
Therefore, the vector spaces of tubes can be described as
\mathrm{T}_{a;b}=\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\;\mathrm{Z}_{j}(a)\right]\mathclose{}
for
b\in\mathcal{X}_{jj}
, as long as the above assumption on
\mathrm{J}
stands.

When
\mathcal{X}
is a spherical fusion category, the above specializes to the
tube algebra

\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})
, which is a symmetric Frobenius algebra whose representations realize the Drinfeld center of
\mathcal{X}
.
The corresponding claim for multifusion setting is straightforward, but if we allow for
\mathcal{X}
to have infinitely many isomorphism classes of simple objects,
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})
is no longer a symmetric Frobenius algebra, since it is not unital.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a spherical semisimple multitensor category, and let
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}\subset\mathrm{I}\subset\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
be in the diagonal part as in Definition
3.10
.
The vector space

\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})\coloneqq\bigoplus_{a,b\in\mathrm{I}}\mathrm{T}_{a;b}=\bigoplus_{a,b\in\mathrm{I}}\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\,\overline{x}\,a\,x\right]\mathclose{}

is endowed with the structure of an associative
\Bbbk
-algebra with local units. The product is given by welding of tube elements, i.e., for
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\overline{x}ax\right]\mathclose{}
and
g\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{c}\,\overline{y}by\right]\mathclose{}

f\cdot g\coloneqq\mathrm{w}(f\otimes g)=\star_{xy}(f\circ_{b}g)

which is associative by Proposition
3.11
.
Now, given a finite set
F\subset\mathrm{I}
, multiplication by the idempotent

\mathtt{e}_{F}\coloneqq\;\sum_{a\in F}\,\mathtt{e}_{a}\in\bigoplus_{a\in F}\,\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\,a\right]\mathclose{}\,.

from both sides projects
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
to
\bigoplus_{a,b\in F}\mathrm{T}_{a;b}
.

Definition 3.13
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a spherical semisimple multitensor category and
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}\subset\mathrm{I}\subset\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
be in the diagonal part as in Definition
3.10
. The associative
\Bbbk
-algebra with local units
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
is called the
tube algebra of
\mathcal{X}
.

In particular, a homogeneous element of the tube algebra
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\overline{x}ax\right]\mathclose{}
can be depicted as

which justifies the terminology.

The tube algebra comes with a symmetric linear form given by the trace coming from the spherical structure of
\mathcal{X}
, defined by

\epsilon\colon\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})\to\Bbbk,\qquad\epsilon(f)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{tr}_{a}(f)&\text{if $f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\,\mathbf{1}_{i}a\mathbf{1}_{i}\right]\mathclose{}$},\\
0&\text{if $f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\overline{x}ax\right]\mathclose{}$, $x\neq\mathbf{1}_{i}$ or $a\neq b$,}\end{cases}

where
a\in\mathcal{X}_{i}
and we interpret
\mathrm{tr}_{a}
as a scalar by (
2.1
).
In the case that
\mathcal{X}
is fusion and
\mathrm{I}
is finite,
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
is a Frobenius algebra

\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})^{*}\cong\bigoplus_{a,b\in\mathrm{I}}\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[a\,x\,\overline{b}\,\overline{x}\right]\mathclose{}^{*}\cong\bigoplus_{a,b\in\mathrm{I}}\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[x\,b\,\overline{x}\,\overline{a}\right]\mathclose{}\cong\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})\,.

4
Tube algebra representations

The goal of this section is to explicitly define a braided monoidal structure on the category
\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
of tube algebra representations of a spherical semisimple multitensor category
\mathcal{X}
. In Section
5
this structure is related to the naturally induced on the Drinfeld center of the ind-completion of
\mathcal{X}
.

4.1
Tensor product of representations

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a spherical semisimple multitensor category and suppose we are given
\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}\subset\mathrm{I}\subset\operatorname{Iso}\mathcal{X}
in the diagonal part as in Definition
3.10
.
Every tube algebra representation
M\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
admits a canonical decomposition

M\cong\bigoplus_{a\in\mathrm{I}}\,M_{a},\quad\text{ where}\quad M_{a}\coloneqq M.\mathtt{e}_{a}

determined by the action of the local units
\mathtt{e}_{a}
.

In order to define the tensor product of two tube algebra representations, we will consider the following auxiliary space

\Pi_{a,b{;}c}\coloneqq\mathrm{T}_{ab;c}=\bigoplus_{x\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\,\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{c}\,\overline{x}\,a\,b\,x\right]\mathclose{}

(4.1)

where
a
and
b
represent the degree of the vectors of the representations and
c
the label where the tube algebra acts.

Proposition 4.1
.

The tube algebra
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
acts from the right on
\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
via

\pi.f\coloneqq\mathrm{w}(\pi\otimes f)=\star_{yx}(\pi\circ_{c}f)

(4.2)

for
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{d}\,\overline{y}\,c\,y\right]\mathclose{}
and
\pi\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{c}\,\overline{x}\,a\,b\,x\right]\mathclose{}
.

Proof.

The module associativity follows from Proposition
3.11
. Locality is ensured by taking the sum of the idempotents
\mathtt{e}_{c}
for each basis element
\pi\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{c}\,\overline{x}\,a\,b\,x\right]\mathclose{}
in a finite-dimensional
W\subset\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
.
∎

Now, given tube algebra representations
M,N\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
and
c\in\mathrm{I}
define the vector space

(M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N)_{c}\coloneqq\bigoplus_{a,b\in\mathrm{I}}\,M_{a}\otimes N_{b}\otimes\Pi_{a,b{;}c}

A homogeneous vector
m\otimes n\otimes\pi\in M_{a}\otimes N_{b}\otimes\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
is graphically depicted as

{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{{}}{}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -47.24 0 L 47.24 0 M -47.24 0 L -47.24 39.37 M 47.24 0 L 47.24 39.37 M -47.24 39.37 L 47.24 39.37}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

The tube algebra action on
\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
defines an action on
M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N
. However, we need to account for the actions on the representations
M
and
N
. To this end, we define an equivalence relation on
M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N
:

(i)

f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\,\overline{u}a^{\prime}u\right]\mathclose{}

m\in M_{a^{\prime}}

n\in N_{b}
and
\pi\in\Pi_{a,b{;}c}

(4.4)

for
(\alpha,\overline{\alpha})
a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\,\overline{v}\tilde{a}v\right]\mathclose{}
.

Definition 4.2
.

Given tube algebra representations
M,N\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
, their
tensor product
is defined as the quotient

M{\,\Box\,}N\coloneqq{\mathchoice{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\displaystyle{M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83437pt}{$\displaystyle{\sim}$}}{\raisebox{3.41666pt}{$\textstyle{M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.83437pt}{$\textstyle{\sim}$}}{\raisebox{2.60417pt}{$\scriptstyle{M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-1.34427pt}{$\scriptstyle{\sim}$}}{\raisebox{2.0487pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{M\overset{\sim}{{\,\Box\,}}N}$}\mkern-5.0mu\diagup\mkern-4.0mu\raisebox{-0.99101pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle{\sim}$}}}

(4.5)

where the equivalence relation
\sim
is defined by (
4.3
) and (
4.4
).

Remark 4.3
.

In the setting of tensor categories, the summand of
x=\mathbf{1}
in (
4.1
) is often used to describe the monoidal product, which can be interpreted as a variation of the Day convolution product, see for example
[
16
, Section 3]
.
While it is possible to reduce the computation to the case
x=\mathbf{1}_{i}
for some
i
(see Proposition
4.7
(iii)), we chose to work with this more flexible presentation because there is no preferred choice of the
0
-cell
i\in\Gamma
, and the braiding will inevitably introduce nontrivial labels
x
.

Remark 4.4
.

The previously defined relations can be also graphically expressed in terms of tube-like notation: the relation starting from an action on
M

Proposition 4.5
.

Let
M,N\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
be tube algebra representations.
The tube algebra action (
4.2
) on
\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
descends to an action on the tensor product
M{\,\Box\,}N
.

Proof.

We need to verify that the action is compatible with the relations defining the quotient
M{\,\Box\,}N
.

For the first relation (
4.3
), notice that

{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\right).

Applying Lemma
3.9
(ii) we obtain the expression

\sum_{t,\tilde{b},z\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}m\otimes n.\overline{\beta}_{j}\otimes\star_{zy}\circ(\star_{ux})_{z}\left[(\beta^{j}\circ_{u}g)\circ_{ab}\pi\circ_{c}f\right]=\sum_{\tilde{b}\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}m\otimes n.\overline{\beta}_{\!j}\otimes\star_{ux}\left[(\beta^{j}\circ_{u}g)\circ_{ab}\pi\right].f

proving the desired result. A similar argument shows the compatibility of the tube algebra action with the relation (
4.4
).
∎

Proposition 4.6
.

The tensor product from Definition
4.2
extends to a functor

{\,\Box\,}\colon\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})\times\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})\to\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})

given for homomorphisms
F\colon M\to M^{\prime}
and
G\colon N\to N^{\prime}
between tube algebra representations by the assignment

\displaystyle F{\,\Box\,}G\colon

\displaystyle M{\,\Box\,}N

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle M^{\prime}{\,\Box\,}N^{\prime}\,,

\displaystyle m\otimes n\otimes\pi

\displaystyle\mapsto

\displaystyle F(m)\otimes G(n)\otimes\pi

that, in particular, is a well-defined homomorphism of tube algebra representations.

Proof.

A routine check shows that
F{\,\Box\,}G
preserves the relations (
4.3
) and (
4.4
).
Since the action (
4.2
) is solely defined on
\pi
it is clear that
F{\,\Box\,}G
is an intertwiner.
∎

(4.9)

Now, since the product of tube algebra elements is
\overline{\mu}_{i}\cdot\overline{\alpha}_{k}=\star_{\overline{x}x}(\overline{\mu}_{i}\circ_{t}\overline{\alpha}_{k})
, we obtain by Lemma
3.9
(v) that

\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{d}_{t}\star_{\overline{x}x}(\overline{\mu}_{i}\circ_{t}\overline{\alpha}_{k})\otimes\alpha^{k}\circ_{t}\mu^{i}\circ_{xx}\mathtt{e}_{x}=\mathrm{d}_{x}^{2}\mathrm{d}_{x}^{-1}\langle\mathtt{e}_{x},\mathtt{e}_{x}\rangle\,\overline{\eta}_{i}\otimes\eta^{i}\circ_{\mathbf{1}}\mathtt{e}_{x}

where
(\overline{\eta},\eta)
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\,\tilde{a}\right]\mathclose{}
.

4.9
) we get the expression

Proposition 4.9
.

\mathrm{A}_{M,N,L}
is a well-defined natural isomorphism of
\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
-representations.

Proof.

Naturality is immediate from the definition.
It follows from Proposition
3.11
and the definition of the tube algebra action (
4.2
) that
\mathrm{A}_{M,N,L}
is an intertwiner. To check that the associator is well-defined under relation (
4.3
), notice that on one hand

(m\otimes n\otimes\pi.f)\otimes l\otimes\rho\in M_{a}\otimes N_{b}\otimes{\Pi_{a{,}b{;}c}}\otimes L_{d}\otimes{\Pi_{c{,}d{;}r}}

gets assigned by
\mathrm{A}_{M,N,L}
the value

(4.12)

It follows from Lemma
3.8
and
3.6
that

\sum_{{t}\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{d}_{{t}}\,(\overline{\beta}_{j}\cdot\overline{\alpha}_{i})\otimes\alpha^{i}\circ_{{t}}\beta^{j}=\mathrm{d}_{z}\mathrm{d}_{y}\sum_{u\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\overline{\gamma}_{k}\otimes\overline{\nu_{i}}\circ_{u}\gamma^{k}\circ_{\overline{u}}\nu_{i}

where
(\overline{\gamma},\gamma)
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{d}\,\overline{u}\,\tilde{d}u\right]\mathclose{}
and
(\overline{\nu},\nu)
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{z}\,\overline{y}\,u\right]\mathclose{}
. Applying this formula and Lemma
3.9
(ii) to the expression (
4.12
) we obtain (
4.11
). That the associator is well-defined under relation (
4.4
) can be verified using analogous arguments.

Lemma 4.10
.

M,N,L
be tube algebra representations. Then, it holds that

\mathrm{A}_{M,N,L}\left[\left(m\otimes n\otimes\hbox to49.8pt{\vbox to47.54pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 24.9004pt\lower-13.81044pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

.

4.3
Monoidal unit and dualizable objects

Definition 4.12
.

Define the
trivial tube algebra representation

\mathbb{I}
as the vector space

\bigoplus_{a\in\mathrm{I}}\;\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\mathbf{1}\right]\mathclose{}

with tube algebra action given by the partial trace

l.f\coloneqq\mathrm{d}_{x}\,\,\mathrm{ptr}_{x}(l\circ_{a}f)

for
l\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{a}\,\mathbf{1}\right]\mathclose{}
and
f\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\overline{x}ax\right]\mathclose{}
.

Remark 4.13
.

In case
\mathcal{X}
is a tensor category and we consider the tube algebra associated to the index set
\mathrm{I}=\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, the trivial representation is one-dimensional and the action is given by the full trace.

The trivial representation
\mathbb{I}
serves as monoidal unit for the tensor product (
4.5
). In order to show this, define the
right unitor
morphism by the assignment

\mathbf{r}_{M}\colon M\to M\,{\,\Box\,}\,\mathbb{I},\qquad m_{a}\mapsto m_{a}\otimes\mathtt{e}_{\mathbf{1}}\otimes\mathtt{e}_{a}

and, similarly, the
left unitor
morphism as

\mathbf{l}_{M}\colon M\to\mathbb{I}\,{\,\Box\,}\,M,\qquad m_{a}\mapsto\mathtt{e}_{\mathbf{1}}\otimes m_{a}\otimes\mathtt{e}_{a}\,.

Proposition 4.14
.

For any tube algebra representation
M\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
, the unitors
\mathbf{r}_{M}
and
\mathbf{l}_{M}
are well-defined isomorphisms of tube algebra representations.

Proof.

Given
m\in M_{a}
,
l\in\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{b}\,\mathbf{1}\right]\mathclose{}
and
\pi\in\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
, we have that

m\otimes l\otimes\pi\overset{\eqref{eq:Rel2}}{\sim}m\otimes\mathtt{e}_{\mathbf{1}}\otimes l\circ_{b}\pi\overset{\eqref{eq:Rel1}}{\sim}m.l\circ_{b}\pi\otimes\mathtt{e}_{\mathbf{1}}\otimes\mathtt{e}_{c}

and thus
(M\,{\,\Box\,}\,\mathbb{I})_{c}\cong M_{c}
, for every
c\in\mathrm{I}
. Moreover, relation (
4.3
) ensures that
\mathbf{r}_{M}
is an intertwiner. A similar argument shows the statement for
\mathbf{l}_{M}
.
∎

Proposition 4.15
.

The triangle axiom holds, i.e., the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(M{\,\Box\,}\mathbb{I}){\,\Box\,}N}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M{\,\Box\,}(\mathbb{I}\,{\,\Box\,}N)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M{\,\Box\,}N}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{A}_{M,\mathbb{I},N}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbf{r}_{M}{\,\Box\,}\mathrm{id}_{N}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{M}{\,\Box\,}\mathbf{l}_{N}}

commutes for all tube algebra representations
M
and
N
.

Proof.

From Lemma
4.10
it follows that

\mathrm{A}_{M,\mathbb{I},N}\circ\mathbf{r}_{M}{\,\Box\,}\mathrm{id}_{N}(m\otimes n\otimes\pi)=m\otimes(\mathtt{e}_{\mathbf{1}}\otimes n\otimes\mathtt{e}_{b})\otimes\pi=\mathrm{id}_{M}{\,\Box\,}\mathbf{l}_{N}(m\otimes n\otimes\pi)

for any
m\otimes n\otimes\pi\in M_{a}\otimes N_{b}\otimes\Pi_{a,b{;}c}
, which proves the desired result.
∎

Now that we count with a monoidal unit in
\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
, we can discuss dualizability of representations. From the infinite nature of this tensor category we know that not every representation admits a dual object.

Definition 4.16
.

A tube algebra representation
M\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
is called
locally finite
when
M_{a}
is finite-dimensional for every
a\in\mathrm{I}
and the support
\{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}\,|\,M_{t}\neq 0\}
is finite.

Remark 4.17
.

In the case that
\mathrm{I}=\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, the situation simplifies. We have that locally finite representations are actually finite-dimensional.

To define the dual of a locally finite representation, we make use of the following involutive structure on the tube algebra: given
a,b\in\mathrm{I}
the assignment

Definition 4.18
.

Let
M\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
be a locally finite tube algebra representation. The
dual tube algebra representation of
M
is a triple consisting of:

(
i
)

The representation
\overline{M}
given for
a\in\mathrm{I}
by the vector space
\overline{M}_{a}\coloneqq M_{\,\overline{a}}^{*}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Bbbk}(M_{\,\overline{a}},\Bbbk)
with tube algebra action

\varphi.f(m)\coloneqq\varphi\left(m.f^{\#}\right)

for
\varphi\in M_{\,\overline{a}}^{*}
, any tube element
f\in\mathrm{T}_{a,b}
and
m\in M_{\,\overline{b}}
.

(
ii
)

after applying the identity (
3.9
). We obtain by means of (
3.8
) the expression

\mathrm{d}_{x}\;\varphi\left(m.\left(\overline{\eta}_{k}^{\#}\cdot f^{\#}\right)\right)\otimes\mathrm{ptr}_{x}\left(\eta^{k}\circ_{ab}\pi\right)=\mathrm{ev}_{M}\left(\varphi.f\otimes m\otimes\pi\right)

for
(\overline{\eta},\eta)
a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[a\,b\right]\mathclose{}
. Compatibility with relation (
4.4
) follows analogously. A routine check shows that
\mathrm{ev}_{M}
is an intertwiner of tube algebra representations. To prove that
\mathrm{coev}_{M}
is compatible with the action requires a more involved calculation using (
4.8
).
We check now the snake relation. By direct computation one can verify that the composition

M\xrightarrow{\;\mathbf{l}_{M}\;}\mathbb{I}{\,\Box\,}M\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{coev}_{M}{\,\Box\,}\mathrm{id}\;}\left(M{\,\Box\,}\overline{M}\right){\,\Box\,}M\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{A}_{M,\overline{M},M}\;}M{\,\Box\,}\left(\overline{M}{\,\Box\,}M\right)\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{id}{\,\Box\,}\mathrm{ev}_{M}\;}M{\,\Box\,}\mathbb{I}\xrightarrow{\;\mathbf{r}_{M}^{-1}\;}M

assigns to a vector
m\in M_{a}
the value

\sum_{t\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{d}_{t}\;\sum_{i}\left(\overline{m}_{t}^{i}.\eta^{k}\right)(m)\;m_{t}^{i}.\overline{\eta}_{k}=\sum_{j}\overline{m}_{a}^{j}(m)\;m_{a}^{j}=m

where
(\eta,\overline{\eta})
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[a\,t\right]\mathclose{}

and the first equality follows from Lemma
3.7
(i) and the independence of the coevaluation map from the choice of basis. The second equality follows by the definition of the dual basis to
\{m_{a}^{j}\}_{j}
. The remaining snake relation holds similarly.
∎

provides the inverse braiding

According to Lemma
3.9
(v) we have that

\sum_{\tilde{c}\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{d}_{\tilde{c}}\,\overline{\gamma}_{k}\cdot\overline{\eta}_{j}\otimes(\eta^{j}\circ_{\tilde{c}}\gamma^{k})\circ_{a}\mathtt{e}_{a}=\mathrm{d}_{a}^{2}\;\overline{\zeta}_{i}\otimes\mathtt{e}_{a}\circ_{\mathbf{1}}\zeta^{i}

where
(\overline{\zeta},\zeta)
is a pair of dual bases of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[\overline{t}\,c\right]\mathclose{}
, but since
c\in\operatorname{Irr}\mathcal{X}
, it follows that
t=c
. We can choose the bases
\zeta=\mathrm{id}_{c}
and
\overline{\zeta}=\mathrm{d}_{c}^{-1}\mathrm{id}_{c}
to finally conclude that the expressions (
4.18
) and (
4.17
) agree. In a similar manner, one can verify the second hexagon axiom.
∎

Definition 4.25
.

The
twist
of
M\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
is given by the assignment

\Theta_{M}\colon M\to M,\quad m_{a}\mapsto m_{a}.\mathtt{\tau}_{a}\;.

Proposition 4.26
.

\Theta
defines a twist on
\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
in the sense of

[
8
, Definition 8.10.1]
.

Proof.

It is clear that
\Theta_{M}
is a natural isomorphism, with inverse given by the action of the inverse twist element. That
\Theta_{M}
is an intertwiner follows from (
4.14
). Given tube algebra representations
M,N\in\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
, one can check that
\Theta_{M}{\,\Box\,}\Theta_{N}\circ\mathrm{B}_{N,M}\circ\mathrm{B}_{M,N}
and
\Theta_{M{\,\Box\,}N}
agree, by a direct computation involving (
4.14
) and Lemma
3.8
.
∎

Theorem 4.27
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a spherical semisimple multitensor category. The data
\left({\,\Box\,},\mathbb{I},\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\Theta\right)
endow the
\Bbbk
-linear category
\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
with the structure of a braided monoidal category with twist. Moreover, the full
\Bbbk
-linear subcategory
\operatorname{Rep}^{\mathrm{l.f.}}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
of locally finite tube algebra representations is a ribbon semisimple tensor category.

Proof.

The statement compiles the results of Proposition
4.6
,
4.11
,
4.24
and
4.26
. The rigidity of the subcategory
\operatorname{Rep}^{\mathrm{l.f.}}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X},\mathrm{I})
was shown in Proposition
4.19
. It remains to be checked that
\Theta_{\overline{M}}=\overline{\Theta_{M}}
. A computation similar to (
4.19
) shows that for
\varphi\in\overline{M}_{a}
it holds that

\overline{\Theta_{M}}(\varphi)=\textstyle{\sum_{j}}\;\varphi(m_{a}^{j}.\mathtt{\tau}_{a})\;\overline{m}_{a}^{j}\,,

but, since
\mathtt{\tau}_{a}^{\#}=\mathtt{\tau}_{\overline{a}}
and
\{m_{a}^{j}\}
and
\{\overline{m}_{a}^{j}\}
are dual bases, the result folows.
∎

). To this end, consider for central objects

represents its image under the composition
\Psi_{Y,X}\circ\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{E}(X),\mathrm{E}(Y)}
.
Now, by applying naturality of
\sigma^{X}
, we can transport
m
to bound
\overline{\varphi}_{k}
. Next, by means of (
3.8
), we further transport
m
to the right side of
n
obtaining bases
\overline{\psi}
and
\psi
of
\mathrm{H}\mathopen{}\left[X\,\overline{z}\right]\mathclose{}
in the process. By naturality of
\sigma^{X}
and
\sigma^{Y}
the bases
\overline{\psi}
and
\psi
are glued together and using (
3.9
), we finally recover the expression (
5.8
), thereby proving that
\mathrm{E}
is braided.
∎

Let us summarize what we have obtained so far.

Theorem 5.3
.

Let
\mathcal{X}
be a spherical semisimple multitensor category. There is a braided monoidal equivalence

\mathrm{E}\colon\mathcal{Z}(\operatorname{Ind}\mathcal{X})\xrightarrow{\hskip 8.19447pt\simeq\hskip 8.19447pt}\operatorname{Rep}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})

given by the assignment (
5.1
) and monoidal structure (
5.2
). Moreover, restricting
\mathrm{E}
to dualizable objects, we obtain an equivalence

\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{X})\xrightarrow{\hskip 8.19447pt\simeq\hskip 8.19447pt}\operatorname{Rep}^{\rm l.f.}\mathrm{Tube}(\mathcal{X})

of ribbon semisimple tensor categories.
